findings.section: Design > Readiness, and why each wait is there (lines 273-339) AND Design > One config, two projects (lines 136-146)
findings.title: Readiness waits carry no timeouts, and the obvious fix is silently capped at 30 s
findings.merged_from: adversarial (P0, conf 100) + feasibility (P1, conf 100) - agreed by two independently dispatched contexts
findings.scenario: You hand this spec to someone and they write the eleven screenshot tests exactly as printed. Each shot opens /play and waits up to FIVE SECONDS for the score to draw and for Play to light up - while every test already in web/e2e gives those same two signals 30 and 60 seconds. They notice, copy the 60_000 in, push, and the run still dies at exactly 30 seconds with 'Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded', because the config never raises the per-test budget, so any ceiling above 30 s is decoration. The gate blocks merge, so a red run stops everyone.
findings.whats_wrong: The readiness code block passes no timeout, so every assertion inherits Playwright's 5000 ms default expect timeout (web/playwright.e2e.config.ts sets no `expect` block and no top-level `timeout`). The same signals in the repo today use 30_000 and 60_000. WORSE: writing 60_000 into the spec does not fix it, because the per-test default of 30_000 ms kills the test first.
findings.before_1:
**The eight player-loaded shots** (bundled beat, long score, both popovers, transport toggles,
ghost hover, tooltip over the header, narrow viewport):

```ts
await expect(page.getByTestId('notation-surface').locator('svg').first()).toBeVisible();
await expect(page.getByTestId('transport-play')).toBeEnabled(); // engine + soundfont ready
await expect(page.getByRole('progressbar', { name: 'Loading the player' })).toHaveCount(0);
```

findings.why_it_works: The three numbers are not invented: they are what the same states already needed against the same build (a11y.e2e.ts:104/:119 = 30_000 on the svg, :161/:190 = 60_000 on transport-play, :152 = 15_000 on engine-error, :141 = no timeout on the skeleton). The per-project timeout is the mechanism that makes them reachable, and it is scoped to `chromium` so no existing behaviour test gets a looser budget.
findings.spike:
RAN. Two throwaway Playwright projects in the scratchpad, using the repo's own installed Playwright.
SPIKE 1 - config with NO top-level `timeout` and NO `expect` block; one assertion at { timeout: 60_000 }:
  exit 1, wall clock 31.61 s
  FAIL '60s expect ceiling under the 30s default test timeout (30.0s)'
  'Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded.'
  call log: 'Expect "toBeVisible" with timeout 60000ms'
  => the TEST timeout fired at 30.0 s; the 60 s expect ceiling was requested and is unreachable.
SPIKE 1b - same, plus `timeout: 8_000` on the chromium PROJECT:
  wall clock 8.75 s, FAIL 'Test timeout of 8000ms exceeded' => per-project timeout DOES override the 30 s default.
HARNESS VERIFIED BY ORCHESTRATOR: scratchpad/spike1/playwright.config.ts confirmed to mirror web/playwright.e2e.config.ts in the respect under test (no timeout, no expect block); test-results/ present; repo `git status --porcelain` empty after the runs.
findings.count_resolution: The two reviewers disagreed on how many shots are affected (adversarial 8, feasibility 'at least five'). EIGHT is correct and the spec states it itself at lines 279-280: 'The eight player-loaded shots (bundled beat, long score, both popovers, transport toggles, ghost hover, tooltip over the header, narrow viewport)'. The other three (Landing, Skeleton, Engine error) are in the table at 290-294. 8 + 3 = 11.
findings.unverified_half: 'Most shots time out on every run / permanently red' is NOT verified - only the mechanism is. Settling frequency needs a real `next build` plus a lane run, which was not commissioned. Evidence for: nobody writes 60_000 for something that lands in 3 s, and the whole existing lane does so consistently. Evidence against: the spec's own 60-run measurement reports about 2.2 s per shot (line 110). TREAT AS: the 5 s-vs-30/60 s gap and the unreachable-ceiling are VERIFIED; 'permanently red' is NOT.
findings.alternative_fix: If the maintainer prefers matching existing style over adding config surface: `test.setTimeout(120_000)` inside each *.vr.ts (precedent player.e2e.ts:729). The project-level version is one line instead of eleven and also covers a twelfth shot someone adds later and forgets to annotate. Recommend the project-level form.

findings.title: Footprint omits tooling/workflow-guards.test.mjs, whose assertions this plan breaks
findings.scenario: You implement the gate, run the whole lint-and-test set locally, push, and the push goes through clean. Then CI turns red in a job you did not touch: a Node test file under tooling/ has been pinning the exact wording of the step you just deleted, and it fails because that line is gone. You cannot reproduce it with git push - the pre-push hook runs the tests package-by-package and pnpm leaves the repo root out of that list, so the one script that runs this file is never reached.
findings.whats_wrong: tooling/workflow-guards.test.mjs pins today's e2e job in source. Two assertions BREAK and two more constrain the new job. The spec never mentions the file (grep 'workflow-guards' over the spec returns nothing), while its footprint names .github/workflows/ci.yml. It runs only via the ROOT `pnpm run test:tooling` (ci.yml:105, inside the `quality` job that ci-green needs), and the pre-push hook cannot reach it.

findings.section: Process changes this carries, the web/e2e/*.vr.ts bullet (lines 549-552)
findings.title: 'The config cannot survive zero shots' is false on the path CI actually uses
findings.scenario: Picture the gate landing in two steps - the config and CI job first, the eleven screenshots a week later. You expect that gap to be loud, because the spec promises the run exits 1 with 'No tests found'. It does not. The unscoped command CI runs still finds all the existing behaviour tests, so the run goes green, the web job reports success, ci-green is satisfied, and a merge-blocking visual gate sits in the workflow covering exactly zero pixels. The only command that would have shouted is the local one nobody runs in CI.
findings.whats_wrong: Playwright raises 'No tests found' only when the WHOLE root suite is empty. CI is deliberately unscoped, so the 44 existing *.e2e.ts tests keep the root suite non-empty and the run exits 0 with an empty chromium project. Only the local scoped `test:vr` exits 1.

  and this is the one entry whose absence the config cannot survive: a scoped run whose `testMatch`
  finds nothing exits 1 with "No tests found". Loud rather than silent, but it means the config and
  the CI step cannot land before the first shot exists.
findings.why_it_works: It replaces a fake mechanical barrier with a real one, in a file the repo already uses for exactly this shape of guard, inside the job ci-green waits on. Repo precedent for 'prove the fence actually fires': tooling/check-core-purity-canary.sh and web/scripts/assert-design-system-css.mjs, both named in AGENTS.md. Caveat inherited from F-2: a tooling/ test gates CI but not the push.

findings.section: Design > Readiness, and why each wait is there (lines 273-339) + the shots table row at line 202
findings.title: The long-score shot photographs the bundled beat, and its toast wait passes vacuously
findings.merged_from: feasibility (P1, conf 75) - verifier raised effective confidence to 100 from source
findings.scenario: You write the long-score shot the way any screenshot test is written - get to /play, wait until the player is actually ready, THEN pick Punk.gp. All three readiness waits are already satisfied at that moment, so they return instantly; the toast wait returns instantly too, because the toast does not exist yet; half a second later Playwright takes the picture. What you get is the BUNDLED BEAT with a spinner toast over it - and the first run writes that as the baseline, so the shot goes green forever and never once looks at a long score.
findings.whats_wrong: /play already shows the bundled beat before any file is opened, so the svg is visible, transport-play is enabled and the loading bar is gone BEFORE the file is picked. Everything after setInputFiles is asynchronous. So every prescribed wait passes on its first poll - including the toast's toHaveCount(0), because the toast does not exist yet. The scroll check, the only signal that proves the swap happened, is mentioned ONCE in passing at line 301 ('after the scroll check') and never listed among the shot's waits.
findings.reachability: JUDGED, not assumed. Ordering B (wait for player, then pick - the natural VR order): all four waits pass before the swap begins, EVERY RUN. transport-play is `disabled={!playerReady}` (PlayerShell.tsx:707) and `opening` does not re-disable it. The repo's own measurement bounds the toast: PlayerShell.tsx:428-429 records the toast reaching the DOM 188 ms after the pick under a 20x CPU throttle, while Playwright's first poll lands within a few ms. toHaveScreenshot's two-identical-samples rule does NOT save it: while the synchronous parse blocks the main thread the page is perfectly static, so two consecutive samples of the WRONG frame match. Ordering A (copy a11y's order - goto, pick, then waits): safe on score identity because `opening` feeds `loadingPlayer` so the progressbar outlasts the open, but still unsafe on render completion - AlphaTab re-renders Punk.gp's 1,026 px asynchronously after setNotation. SOMETIMES, on a slower runner where the re-render exceeds ~1.2 s. VERDICT: every run in ordering B, sometimes in ordering A.
findings.before:
**The long-score shot needs one more wait, and it is not optional.** Opening a file raises a Sonner
toast - `toast.loading('Opening ...')` then `toast.success('... loaded')` (`PlayerShell.tsx:432`
and `:467`) - and a Sonner toast dismisses itself after 4 000 ms. Neither call sets a duration. So
whether the toast is whole, half-faded or already gone at shot time depends on how fast that machine
parsed `Punk.gp`: a guaranteed flake, and the one shot in this list that opens a file. Wait for it to
go, after the scroll check:
findings.after:
**The long-score shot needs two more waits, and the first one is what proves it photographed the
right score.** `/play` already shows the bundled beat, so the svg is visible, `transport-play` is
enabled and the loading bar is gone **before the file is picked**. The open is entirely asynchronous
after `setInputFiles` returns - `OpenFileControl.tsx:69` awaits `readNotation`, then
`PlayerShell.tsx:431` flips `opening` - so every wait in the block above passes on its first poll,
and so does `toHaveCount(0)` on the toast, because the toast does not exist yet (measured at
`PlayerShell.tsx:428`: 188 ms to reach the DOM under a 20x throttle). The shot would be taken 500 ms
after the pick, on the bundled beat with a spinner over it, and the two-identical-samples rule does
not catch it: the parse blocks the main thread, so two consecutive samples of that wrong frame
match. Prove the new score is drawn, the way `a11y.e2e.ts:121-123` already does:

```ts
const surface = page.getByTestId('notation-surface');
await expect
  .poll(() => surface.evaluate((el) => el.scrollHeight > el.clientHeight), { timeout: 30_000 })
  .toBe(true);
```

This is also what makes the toast wait below mean anything: the poll cannot pass until the swap has
committed, so by then the toast exists and `toHaveCount(0)` really waits for it to go.

[then the ORIGINAL toast paragraph continues WORD-FOR-WORD from 'Opening a file raises a Sonner' - deliberately preserved so F-6's edit composes on top without conflict]

findings.section: Design > The shots, 'The navigation is shared, not copied' (lines 183-192) + footprint lines 547-548
findings.title: player-states.ts cannot hold both lanes' contracts - and the spec contradicts itself
findings.scenario: You sit down to write web/e2e/player-states.ts and hit the Skeleton state first. The accessibility test needs the stalled engine module to resume after five seconds; your screenshot needs it to never resume at all, or the state moves while Playwright is sampling it. One exported function cannot do both - and when you get to the long-score state it happens again in the opposite direction: the accessibility test waits for the toast to be fully PAINTED, your shot waits for it to be GONE.
findings.whats_wrong: 'one exported function per state, each returning once that state is reached' + 'both lanes import it' + 'No change to what it asserts' cannot all be true. THE SPEC ALREADY CONTRADICTS ITSELF: lines 183-186 say the shared function returns once the state is reached, while lines 327-330 say the Skeleton shot's route handler 'must stall indefinitely rather than resume after a fixed delay the way the accessibility lane's 5 000 ms stall does'. Three conflicts, all confirmed in the real source: (a) the skeleton stall Infinity vs 5000 ms; (b) the toast - a11y's settleToasts waits for opacity 1, the pixel lane waits for count 0; (c) a11y's bundled-beat test waits on the svg only, the pixel lane also wants transport-play enabled and the progressbar at 0. Note the spec never mentions settleToasts at all (grep: zero hits), so conflict (b) is invisible in the document.

option_A.label: A - player-states.ts exports NAVIGATION ONLY
option_A.what: Each function performs the goto, clicks and file-picks that REACH a state and returns immediately. The Skeleton helper takes its stall duration as an argument. Each lane keeps its own readiness waits where they are today.
option_A.why: The thing that actually drifts on a test-id rename IS the navigation, and the spec's own risk argument (lines 189-192) is specifically about navigation drift producing 'a red VR run whose quickest route to green is regenerating the baselines'. A stale READINESS locator fails loudly with 'locator not found' - red, obvious, no temptation to regenerate. So A shares exactly the half where the dangerous failure mode lives.
option_A.cost: Readiness test-ids stay duplicated across two files (notation-surface, transport-play, notation-skeleton, engine-error, tempo-percent). Renaming one still lands twice. The pixel lane re-derives the timeouts by hand, which is the same hole F-1 is about.
option_A.resolves_a: YES - the parameter is exactly the difference
option_A.resolves_b: YES by construction - the helper never touches toasts
option_A.resolves_c: YES by construction - each lane keeps its own waits
option_A.fixes_F4_free: NO - the scroll poll stays in a11y.e2e.ts only, and a navigation-only gotoLongScore returns before the swap has started, which is precisely the ordering-B failure. F-4 must then be applied as its own edit.
option_A.keeps_footprint_line_548: YES strictly - only goto/click/setInputFiles lines move

option_B.label: B - each function carries navigation AND the reached-state waits
option_B.what: longScoreReady() does the goto, the pick, the svg wait, the scrollHeight>clientHeight poll and settleToasts(). The .vr.ts specs add only shot-specific extras (toast toHaveCount(0), tooltip-open wait, document.fonts.ready, the 500 ms settle).
option_B.why: One source for both the navigation AND the readiness locators and timeouts, so renaming notation-surface or transport-play lands once. It is also the only option under which the pixel lane inherits the proof that the score really swapped.
option_B.cost: The helper must STILL take a per-lane parameter for the Skeleton route, so B does not avoid A's parameter. And a11y's waits are not a superset for every state, so either the helper is strengthened beyond what a11y waits for today (changing a11y's timing) or the pixel lane adds them back as 'extras' - which is A's shape for those states.
option_B.resolves_a: NO - the route handler still has to differ per lane, so B needs the same stallMs parameter A introduces. B is silent on this.
option_B.resolves_b: NO - this is the one conflict B genuinely does not resolve. Lifting a11y's waits verbatim drags settleToasts (opacity 1) into the pixel lane, whose own wait is the opposite (count 0). They COMPOSE sequentially (painted, then four seconds, then gone) so nothing breaks, but the pixel lane inherits an a11y-specific wait and 'verbatim' stops being achievable the moment you carve it out. Also settleToasts returns early when count()===0 (a11y.e2e.ts:85), so placed before the toast exists it is a no-op and does NOT by itself close F-4's vacuous-wait hole.

findings.scenario: You read the spec's reason for the extra toast wait - 'it depends on how fast that machine parsed the file, a guaranteed flake' - and reason from it when you add a twelfth shot that opens a file. But the four-second clock does not start when the file is picked; it starts when the parse FINISHES, so parse speed cancels out entirely. The toast is not a coin flip at all: it is reliably on screen and fully painted when your other waits finish, which is a better reason for the wait than the one written down.
findings.whats_wrong: Sonner's close timer lives in a useEffect whose first line returns while toast.type === 'loading' (sonner 2.0.7, dist/index.mjs:582). So the loading toast never arms a timer. Both calls share the id 'notation-load', so toast.success re-runs that same effect on the same component instance and arms 4000 ms FROM THE SUCCESS CALL, plus 200 ms TIME_BEFORE_UNMOUNT. Dismissal is at parse-completion + 4200 ms.
findings.disagreement_resolution: ADVERSARIAL IS RIGHT, FEASIBILITY IS WRONG. Every one of the shot's other waits also starts from that same instant - setNotation (:465) and setOpening(false) (:466) are the two lines immediately before toast.success (:467). The loading bar reaches gone 700 ms later, document.fonts.ready is instant, the settle is 500 ms. So the shot lands about 1.2 s into a 4.2 s life - a margin of roughly three seconds - and the parse duration cancels out of BOTH sides. Corroborated by the repo's own measurement at client/src/components/ui/Sonner/Sonner.tsx:38-40: 'the Opening... toast was replaced by its success text at 43 ms with opacity still 0.02'. Feasibility's 'nondeterministic at shot time' is not preserved - it is deterministic-PRESENT. A residual tail exists only if you OMIT the wait, and it is the opposite direction from what the spec describes.
findings.false_clause: 'whether the toast is whole, half-faded or already gone at shot time depends on how fast that machine parsed `Punk.gp`: a guaranteed flake'. BOTH halves fail - the dependence on parse speed (the clock starts at parse completion, so it cancels) and 'guaranteed flake' (it is deterministically present and fully painted). Also incomplete: 'a Sonner toast dismisses itself after 4 000 ms' is true of TOAST_LIFETIME but silent on the fact that the clock does not start at toast.loading.
findings.surviving_clauses: 'Neither call sets a duration' (verified, including the Toaster and toastOptions fallbacks - <Toaster /> is bare at web/app/layout.tsx:19 and client Sonner.tsx:32 passes classNames only). TOAST_LIFETIME = 4000. 'needs one more wait, and it is not optional' SURVIVES and is STRENGTHENED: omitting the wait does not produce a flake, it produces a baseline permanently bound to a success toast carrying the filename, over the notation box the shot exists for. 'the one shot in this list that opens a file' and line 308's 'Any shot added later that reaches its state by opening a file needs the same wait' both survive.
